Proline (Pro) is a naturally occurring amino acid.

{{figure:pdf_visual_01.png}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.stem: Proline is often found bonded to glycine (Gly) in a protein.
parts.text:
Draw the dipeptide Pro-Gly.

The peptide bond must be shown fully displayed.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Name the type of reaction that forms a dipeptide from two amino acids.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text:
Proline is able to form a poly(proline) peptide chain.

A section of a poly(proline) chain is shown.

{{figure:pdf_visual_02.png}}

Suggest why the secondary structure of poly(proline) cannot be stabilised by hydrogen bonding.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.stem:
The reaction scheme shows several reactions of proline.

{{figure:pdf_visual_03.png}}
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of proline with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ in reaction 1.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
Proline has a secondary amine functional group.

Secondary amines react with acyl chlorides. For example, dimethylamine reacts with $\text{RCOCl}$ according to the following equation.

{{figure:pdf_visual_04.png}}

Suggest the skeletal structure of $\mathbf{R}$, $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_3$, the product of reaction 2.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Suggest the reagent required for reaction 3.

parts.text:
At pH 6.5, proline exists in aqueous solution as a zwitterion.

Draw the structure of the zwitterion of proline.

Explain how the zwitterion of proline forms.

parts.label: (e)(ii)
parts.text:
The isoelectric point of an amino acid is the pH at which it exists as a zwitterion.

Three of the amino acids in gelatin are proline, alanine and glutamic acid. Their isoelectric points are shown.

{{figure:pdf_visual_12.png}}

A mixture of these amino acids was analysed by electrophoresis using a buffer solution at pH 4.0.

Draw and label three spots on the diagram of the electropherogram to indicate the likely position of each of these three species after electrophoresis.

Explain your answer.

{{figure:pdf_visual_13.png}}

parts.label: (f)
parts.text:
The weak acid ACES is a compound that can be used to make a buffer solution for electrophoresis experiments.

{{figure:pdf_visual_14.png}}

The anion of the sodium salt of ACES, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{N}_2\text{O}_4\text{SNa}$, is a strong base.

A buffer solution is prepared by the following steps.

- $3.50\text{ g}$ of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{N}_2\text{O}_4\text{SNa}$ is dissolved in $100\text{ cm}^3$ of distilled water.
- $50.0\text{ cm}^3$ of $0.200\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ dilute hydrochloric acid is added to the solution.
- The resulting mixture is transferred to a $250.0\text{ cm}^3$ volumetric flask, and the solution made up to the mark.

$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{N}_2\text{O}_4\text{SNa}$ reacts with $\text{HCl}$ with a 1:1 stoichiometry.

The $\text{p}K_{\text{a}}$ of ACES is 6.88 at $298\text{ K}$.

Calculate the pH of the buffer solution formed at $298\text{ K}$.

[$M_{\text{r}}$: $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{N}_2\text{O}_4\text{SNa}$, 204.1]
